title: capacity-triage-and-rapid-node-substitution-rough-draft
content:
Purpose:
This is a working draft runbook for fast triage and surgical capacity injection when we detect degraded GPU/node hardware or sudden capacity shortfalls. Focus: get inference clusters back to usable capacity with minimal model-quality impact and controlled cost. Not a final playbook — contains heuristic decision points and TODOs for automation owners.

Scope and assumptions:
- Applies to production inference clusters (gpu pools) that host hosted API + dedicated workloads.
- Assumes cluster control plane (k8s) and serving runtime can perform graceful connection drain and model shard rebalancing.
- Hardware replacement may be physical (on-prem) or cloud-instance reprovision. Steps note both.
- Safety-first: prefer capacity backfill before destructive replacements when customer traffic is high.

High-level decision matrix (quick):
- If single-gpu hardware alerts but only ~<3% capacity impact and no latency SLO violations: monitor + schedule replace during maintenance window.
- If degraded performance causes >10% tail-latency regressions OR customer errors rising: escalate to incident, trigger rapid substitution.
- If control-plane shows >15% node eviction risk (OOMs, kernel panics): short-circuit to full node evacuation and capacity add.

Triage checklist (first 10 minutes):
- Confirm alert source (Prometheus alert rule id).
- Check dashboards: per-model latency, tail p95/p99, queue length, token-per-second metrics.
- List affected nodes: kubectl get nodes --selector=gpu=true --show-labels; inspect taints/conditions.
- Look for correlated events (deploys, rollout, autoscaler activity) — check CI/CD and rollout window.
- Announce incident to #sre-oncall and relevant product/owner channels with short summary and impact estimate.

Immediate mitigation options (choose one based on impact):
1) Soft-failover: mark problematic nodes as lower-priority target for autoscaler/routing. Apply label: kubectl label node <node> degraded=true --overwrite. Modify routing policy to prefer healthy zones.
2) Drain + Live backfill (preferred when spare capacity exists): kubectl cordon <node>; kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data --grace-period=60. Verify pods reschedule to warm-pool or burst nodes.
3) Emergency scale-up: manually provision warm instances (cloud) or enable hot-spare preprovisioned machines. Use infra-scripts: scripts/provision-hotspare --pool inference-hotpool --count 3 --type g5x (example).

Safe drain checklist:
- Confirm model router fallback is active and configured to send partial traffic to variants (lighter models) if capacity reduces.
- Ensure KV cache snapshots are saved for long-running sessions. Command: curl -X POST $RUNTIME/admin/cache/snapshot
- Increase request timeout tolerance on load-balancer for in-flight streams for 30s to avoid client errors.
- For GPU-backed pods: annotate with safe-drain=true to trigger runtime-specific state flush hooks. kubectl annotate pod <pod> safe-drain=true

Physical GPU replacement (on-prem) - quick sketch:
1) Pre-work: open ticket with hardware team, confirm spare GPU unit serial numbers, schedule ASB window if needed.
2) Cordon node and migrate pods: kubectl cordon <node>; kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data --force --grace-period=60
3) Power down node following datacenter SOP, swap PCIe GPU module, run hardware diagnostics. Document serials.
4) Reboot, verify hardware visible: nvidia-smi -L, check drivers: modinfo nvidia, dmesg for errors.
5) Run local perf smoke (small infer load) and kubelet health checks; remove cordon: kubectl uncordon <node> when stable.

Cloud instance replacement (fast path):
1) If node is host-terminated or underlying instance unhealthy: mark node unschedulable, create new instance from golden image with correct GPU drivers, join cluster.
2) Use node rotation helper: scripts/rotate-node --node <node> --image infra/gpu-golden:v3 --pool inference-pool
3) Verify pods reschedule and runtime warms caches.

KV cache and model routing notes:
- Critical to preserve prefix caches for long conversations. If a pod is drained, attempt to warm new pod with cached KV snapshot pointing to model shard if possible.
- If cache snapshot unavailable, consider temporarily routing affected users to model-variant with smaller context-window instead of failing requests.

Capacity add / warm-pool operations:
- Warm-pool design: maintain a small number of instances per region that have runtimes started but not accepting production traffic. When high-priority drain happens, flip routing via service discovery rather than spin up new runtime from scratch.
- Commands to promote warm pool: scripts/promote-warm --region us-west1 --count 4 --pool inference-warm
- If warm pool exhausted, use burst autoscaling with preemptible pricing but limit to not exceed cost limit: autoscaler set-burst --max-preemptible 12 --cost-bound 20000

Post-incident checklist (during recovery):
- Run smoke tests for baseline models (latency p50/p95 acceptable thresholds).
- Run quality checks for top-5 customer prompts (synth evals) to ensure no model regression after switch.
- Capture logs and export to S3: scripts/export-logs --incident INF-<id> --range 2025-02-19T12:00Z/2025-02-19T13:00Z
- Create a short incident note and assign a POC for follow-up (hardware order, automation work).

Rollback markers and safe states:
- Define safe-state: all pods running, no crashlooping, tail-latency within 5% baseline, no elevated 5xx rate.
- If rollback needed, use a staged rollback for any infra automation: revert autoscaler or node rotation in small groups (1-2 nodes at a time).

Telemetry and alarms to tune (TODOs):
- Add an autoscaler health metric: node-replacement-rate over 1h and alert if >3 (current alerts miss this pattern).
- Add a per-pool cache-miss spike alert (cache_miss_rate > 3x baseline) to catch silent degradation.
- Create synthetic user journeys that exercise long-context flows every 15m.

Runbook gaps / action items (TODO):
- Automate KV cache snapshot/restore in runtime (owner: runtime team, ticket: RUNTIME-654).
- Implement a CLI wrapper that does safe drain + warm-pool promotion in a single command (owner: platform-engineering).
- Document warm-pool sizing for each region (owner: capacity-planning).

Communication templates (copy+paste):
- Incident start (short): "INCIDENT: Inference cluster us-west1 experiencing degraded GPU nodes. Impact: increased tail latency for hosted-api. SRE oncall responding. Initial mitigation: cordon and promote 3 warm nodes. ETA recovery 20-40m."
- Postmortem invite: "Please add any logs, timeline entries, and customer impact notes to INFRA-1987. Blameless postmortem scheduled Thursday 10:30am PT."

Appendix - useful commands (quick):
- kubectl get nodes -l gpu=true -o wide
- kubectl cordon <node> && kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data --grace-period=60
- scripts/rotate-node --node <node> --image <image-tag>
- scripts/promote-warm --region <region> --count <n>
- curl -X POST $RUNTIME/admin/cache/snapshot

Owner and review cadence:
- Primary owner: Aisha Patel (eng-sre)
- Secondary: Marcus Liu (infra)
- Review this doc after next real incident or 30 days, whichever comes first.

Notes: rough language, intentionally prescriptive in places to capture tacit knowledge for oncall. Will break into separate automation runbooks and hardware SOPs in future versions.
